questions.question: What is mocking in unit testing and why do we need it?
questions.title: What is Mocking in Unit Testing | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **Mocking replaces a real dependency with a controlled fake** that you configure to return specific values. It isolates the class under test from its dependencies — database, external APIs, file system — so you test only the unit's logic, not its dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the purpose of mocking, not just how to use it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking mocking means making tests pass without real implementations — missing that it's about isolation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the isolation principle clearly and give a concrete example of what goes wrong without mocking

sections.title: Isolate the Unit Under Test
sections.content: Suppose `OrderService.placeOrder()` calls `InventoryRepository.checkStock()` and `EmailService.sendConfirmation()`. Without mocking: the test requires a real database and mail server — slow, fragile, and tests more than just `placeOrder`. With mocking: replace `InventoryRepository` and `EmailService` with fakes that return configured values. Now we test only `OrderService`'s logic in milliseconds.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Mocking isolates the unit from dependencies
- Fake replaces: DB, external API, filesystem, email service
- Test only the logic of the class under test
- Benefits: fast (ms), no external setup, controlled inputs
- Mockito: the standard Java mocking library
- A mock records interactions — you can verify it was called
- Mocking too much: if you mock everything, you test nothing

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Mocking means replacing a real dependency with a controlled fake. When I'm testing an OrderService, I don't want the test to actually hit a database or send a real email — that would make the test slow, fragile, and dependent on infrastructure. Instead I mock those dependencies using Mockito, configuring them to return specific values for my test scenario. This isolates the test to only the OrderService's logic. The key insight is that a unit test should fail if and only if the unit under test has a bug — not because the database is down.

questions.question: What is Mockito and how do you add it to a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Mockito Setup Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Mockito is the standard Java mocking library.** In Spring Boot, `spring-boot-starter-test` includes Mockito automatically. Add `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` to your test class to enable `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` annotations.

sections.title: Mockito Comes with Spring Boot Test
sections.content: In a Spring Boot project: `spring-boot-starter-test` (test scope) already includes `mockito-core` and `mockito-junit-jupiter`. No manual dependency needed. Activate Mockito annotations with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`. For pure Java projects without Spring: add `mockito-core` and `mockito-junit-jupiter` explicitly. Mockito version 5+ requires Java 11+.

sections.content:
- spring-boot-starter-test includes mockito-core automatically
- @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class): enables @Mock, @InjectMocks
- Pure Java: add mockito-junit-jupiter in test scope
- Mockito 5: requires Java 11+, uses inline mock maker
- mockito-junit-jupiter: JUnit 5 integration extension
- Version compatibility: check Mockito vs JUnit 5 version matrix
- Alternative activation: MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in @BeforeEach

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In a Spring Boot project, Mockito comes included automatically through spring-boot-starter-test which is added to every Spring Boot project as a test scope dependency. To use Mockito annotations in JUnit 5, I add @ExtendWith with MockitoExtension.class to my test class — this tells JUnit to process @Mock, @InjectMocks, and other Mockito annotations before each test. For a plain Java project without Spring Boot, I'd add the mockito-junit-jupiter dependency explicitly in test scope in my pom.xml. The version must be compatible with my JUnit 5 version.

questions.question: When should you NOT mock a dependency?
questions.title: When Not to Mock | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Don't mock value objects, simple utilities, or classes you own that have no side effects.** Don't mock the class under test itself. Don't mock thin wrappers that are trivially tested with real implementation. Over-mocking produces tests that test the test setup, not the code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Testing judgment — knowing limits of mocking is as important as knowing how to use it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking everything including simple value classes, DTOs, and pure functions — wastes setup time and tests nothing real
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'mock only what you don't own' guideline and explain when integration tests are better than heavily mocked unit tests

sections.title: Mock External Dependencies, Not Internal Logic
sections.content: **Mock**: external services (HTTP APIs, database, messaging), slow operations (file I/O, network), non-deterministic behavior (time, random). **Don't mock**: simple value objects (DTOs, entities without behavior), pure utility functions (`StringUtils`, `Math`), the system under test itself, simple collections. **Guideline**: 'only mock what you don't own' — mock third-party dependencies and external systems, use real objects for your own simple classes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Mock: database, external APIs, filesystem, email, time
- Don't mock: DTOs, value objects, your own simple classes
- Don't mock the class being tested
- Don't mock framework classes (List, Map) — use real ones
- Over-mocking: tests that just verify mock interactions, not real behavior
- 'Only mock what you don't own' guideline
- Integration tests: sometimes better than heavily mocked unit tests
- London vs Classical TDD: different philosophies on what to mock

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I follow the principle of only mocking what I don't own or what has external side effects. I mock database repositories, HTTP clients, email services, and anything that's slow or non-deterministic like the current time. I don't mock simple value objects, DTOs, collections, or my own simple utility classes — using real instances is simpler and more meaningful. I also don't mock the class being tested, which sounds obvious but is a mistake I've seen. Over-mocking is a sign that tests are testing the mock setup rather than the actual business logic — if a test only verifies that methods were called on mocks without any real logic being exercised, it's probably over-mocked.

questions.question: What is the difference between mocking and stubbing?
questions.title: Mocking vs Stubbing Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Stubbing** configures a fake to return a specific value (`when().thenReturn()`). **Mocking** (in the verification sense) asserts that a method was called (`verify()`). Mockito objects are both — they can stub return values AND verify interactions. The terms are often used interchangeably in casual speech.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'mock' and 'stub' interchangeably without knowing the distinction
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Gerard Meszaros's test double taxonomy and connect to Mockito's unified approach

sections.title: Stubs Answer Queries; Mocks Verify Calls
sections.content: From Gerard Meszaros's taxonomy: **Stub**: provides canned answers to calls — focuses on state verification ('given this, what does the system return?'). **Mock**: records expectations about interactions — focuses on behavior verification ('was this method called?'). **Mockito**: a Mockito `@Mock` object can do both — configure returns with `when().thenReturn()` (stubbing) AND verify with `verify()` (mocking). In common usage, 'mock' often means any test double.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Stub: provides return values (when.thenReturn)
- Mock: verifies interactions (verify)
- Mockito objects can do both
- Spy: wraps a real object, partially stubs/mocks
- Dummy: placeholder — never used, just fills a parameter
- Fake: working implementation — e.g., in-memory DB
- In practice: 'mock' is used loosely for all test doubles
- State verification (stub) vs behavior verification (mock)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Technically, a stub provides canned return values and is about state verification — you set it up to return certain data and then assert on what the system under test does with that data. A mock is about behavior verification — you assert that specific methods were called on it. In Mockito, a @Mock object can do both: you stub it with when-thenReturn and verify interactions with verify(). In everyday conversation developers use 'mock' loosely for both. If an interviewer wants precision, I'd reference the test double taxonomy: stub, mock, spy, fake, dummy — each with a specific purpose.

questions.question: What is the difference between a test double and a mock?
questions.title: Test Double vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: Test double is the umbrella term for any fake object used in testing; a mock is a specific type of test double that also verifies interactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand testing vocabulary precisely and know that Mockito blurs some of these boundaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using mock and test double interchangeably when they have distinct meanings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all five categories of test doubles (dummy, stub, fake, spy, mock) and explain where Mockito fits

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Test double is the general term coined by Gerard Meszaros — it refers to any object that stands in for a real dependency during a test, just like a stunt double stands in for an actor. There are five distinct categories under that umbrella: dummies are passed around but never really used; stubs provide canned return values; fakes have working implementations but take shortcuts like using an in-memory database; spies wrap real objects and record calls; and mocks are pre-programmed with expectations and verify that specific interactions occurred.

A mock is therefore one specific kind of test double. The key distinction is that mocks do verification — you set up what you expect and the mock will fail your test if those expectations are not met. Stubs, by contrast, just return values without caring whether or how they were called.

Mockito as a framework blurs these lines a bit. When you call Mockito.mock(), it creates an object that can do both stubbing and interaction verification, so Mockito mocks are technically a hybrid. Understanding this distinction matters in interviews because it shows you think clearly about test design, not just framework usage.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Test double is the umbrella term; dummy, stub, fake, spy, mock are the five subtypes
Mocks specifically verify interactions — they fail if expected calls are not made
Stubs only return values; they do not assert anything about how they were called
Mockito.mock() creates a hybrid that can both stub and verify

questions.question: When should you NOT use mocking in unit tests?
questions.title: When Not to Use Mocking
questions.direct_answer: Avoid mocking value objects, the class under test itself, or any dependency so heavily that the test only exercises mock behavior rather than real logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the limits and pitfalls of over-mocking, not just how to create mocks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking every single dependency including simple data objects or the class you are actually testing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the risk of tests that pass even when production code is broken because all the logic is in mock setup

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Mocking is a powerful tool but there are clear cases where it hurts more than it helps. First, never mock value objects or data classes — things like a User POJO, a Money class, or an Address record have no side effects and are cheap to instantiate; mocking them just adds noise. Second, never mock the class under test itself. If you find yourself needing to mock methods on the very class you are testing, that is a sign the class has too many responsibilities and should be split.

Third, avoid over-mocking, which is the most common mistake. When you stub every dependency to return exactly what the code expects, your test can pass even if real integration would fail. You end up testing your mock configuration, not your actual logic.

Fourth, in integration tests you generally want real objects — a real database with H2, a real HTTP client against a WireMock server — because the goal of integration testing is to verify that the pieces work together, and mocks defeat that purpose. A good rule of thumb: mock at the boundary of your system (external services, databases, slow I/O) but use real objects for everything that is pure business logic.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Do not mock value objects or simple POJOs — instantiate them directly
Never mock the class under test; that is a design smell indicating too many responsibilities
Over-mocking produces tests that pass even when production integration would fail
Integration tests should use real or near-real objects, not mocks

questions.question: What is the difference between state-based testing and interaction-based testing, and where does mocking fit?
questions.title: State vs Interaction Testing
questions.direct_answer: State-based testing asserts on the final state of an object; interaction-based testing (where mocking lives) asserts that the right collaborators were called in the right way.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding of why mocking exists as a concept
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every test as interaction-based and over-verifying internal calls
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that interaction tests are fragile and should be reserved for side-effect boundaries like external APIs or messaging

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
There are two philosophies in unit testing. State-based testing says: call the method under test, then assert that the object's state or the return value is what you expect. This is the most common and least fragile style. Interaction-based testing says: assert that the object communicated correctly with its collaborators — meaning it called the right methods with the right arguments. Mockito supports interaction-based testing through its verify() API.

Mocking fits naturally into interaction-based testing because you replace real collaborators with mocks you can observe. For example, if a service sends an email via an EmailSender dependency, you cannot easily inspect the state of the email server in a unit test, so you verify that emailSender.send() was called with the right parameters instead.

The important nuance is that interaction-based tests are more tightly coupled to the implementation than state-based tests. If you refactor a method to use a different collaborator internally but the external behaviour stays the same, a state-based test still passes while an interaction-based test breaks. So a good rule of thumb is: prefer state-based assertions wherever possible, and use interaction-based verification only at side-effect boundaries — things like databases, message queues, external APIs, or email services — where the 'state' lives outside your process and cannot be inspected directly.

sections.title: Key Points
content: State-based: assert on return value or object fields after calling the method.
Interaction-based: assert that collaborators were called correctly using verify().
Mocks enable interaction-based testing by recording and exposing calls.
Prefer state-based tests; use interaction-based only at side-effect boundaries.

questions.question: How does over-mocking harm a test suite, and how do you recognise it?
questions.title: Over-Mocking Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: Over-mocking means mocking classes you own and control, making tests pass even when real integration would fail, and tightly coupling tests to implementation details.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the limits and risks of mocking
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking value objects, DTOs, or simple domain classes that have no side effects
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'only mock types you don't own' heuristic from GOOS (Growing Object-Oriented Software)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Over-mocking happens when you mock things that don't need to be mocked — like simple value objects, pure utility classes, or domain objects that have no side effects. The result is a test that is hard to read, brittle in the face of refactoring, and gives false confidence because it never exercises real logic.

Signs you are over-mocking include: tests that require twenty lines of stubbing before a single assertion, tests that break whenever you rename a private method, and tests that pass even though the production code has a bug because all the interesting logic was stubbed away.

A practical heuristic is 'only mock types you don't own'. Things you don't own are third-party libraries, external APIs, the JDK's IO classes — these are good mocking candidates because you can't control them and they have side effects. Things you do own — your own service classes, domain objects, repositories — should generally be used as real objects or replaced with in-memory fakes rather than mocks.

Another signal is when your test reads more like a transcript of the implementation than a description of the behaviour. If you find yourself stubbing every single collaborator call and then verifying every single collaborator call, you are testing implementation rather than behaviour, which defeats the purpose of the test.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Over-mocking stubs away real logic, giving false confidence.
Signs: excessive setup, fragile tests, tests that mirror implementation.
Heuristic: mock types you don't own; use real objects or fakes for your own classes.
Tests should describe behaviour, not replicate internal call sequences.
